questions.prompt: What information does frequency analysis exploit in a classical substitution cipher?
questions.explanation: Natural languages have nonuniform letter and pattern frequencies that fixed substitutions tend to preserve.
questions.hint: Think about patterns in the language rather than the key format.
questions.newbie: Natural languages have nonuniform letter and pattern frequencies that fixed substitutions tend to preserve.
questions.deep: Natural languages have nonuniform letter and pattern frequencies that fixed substitutions tend to preserve.

questions.prompt: A substitution cipher maps every plaintext A to Q for the whole message. This is best described as…
questions.explanation: A fixed one-to-one replacement alphabet is monoalphabetic substitution.
questions.hint: Does the mapping change from one position to the next?
questions.newbie: A fixed one-to-one replacement alphabet is monoalphabetic substitution.
questions.deep: A fixed one-to-one replacement alphabet is monoalphabetic substitution.

questions.prompt: Why is Vigenère generally harder to analyze than Caesar by simple single-letter frequency alone?
options: Its shift changes with the repeating key
questions.explanation: A repeating keyword applies multiple Caesar-style alphabets, distributing plaintext statistics across positions.
questions.hint: Ask whether every position uses the same shift.
questions.newbie: A repeating keyword applies multiple Caesar-style alphabets, distributing plaintext statistics across positions.
questions.deep: A repeating keyword applies multiple Caesar-style alphabets, distributing plaintext statistics across positions.

questions.prompt: Which observation most strongly suggests a transposition rather than substitution cipher?
options: The same characters appear but their positions look scrambled
questions.explanation: Transposition rearranges positions while preserving the symbols themselves.
questions.hint: Focus on whether symbol identities changed.
questions.newbie: Transposition rearranges positions while preserving the symbols themselves.
questions.deep: Transposition rearranges positions while preserving the symbols themselves.

questions.prompt: What does a Kasiski-style analysis look for in a repeating-key polyalphabetic cipher?
options: Repeated ciphertext patterns that reveal likely key periods
questions.explanation: Repeated plaintext fragments encrypted under the same key alignment can create repeated ciphertext fragments; their spacings can suggest the repeating-key period.
questions.hint: Think about repetition and distance between repeated fragments.

questions.prompt: Why should a stream-cipher keystream be unpredictable to an attacker?
options: Predictable keystream bits can reveal plaintext
questions.explanation: If an attacker can predict the keystream, XOR no longer hides the plaintext effectively.
questions.hint: Remember C=P⊕K.
questions.newbie: If an attacker can predict the keystream, XOR no longer hides the plaintext effectively.
questions.deep: If an attacker can predict the keystream, XOR no longer hides the plaintext effectively.

questions.prompt: In a secure stream-cipher design, the long keystream is normally derived from…
options: a secret key plus appropriate nonce/state
questions.explanation: A compact secret key and nonrepeating public nonce/state are used to generate pseudorandom keystream material.
questions.hint: The keystream is usually generated, not manually stored.
questions.newbie: A compact secret key and nonrepeating public nonce/state are used to generate pseudorandom keystream material.
questions.deep: A compact secret key and nonrepeating public nonce/state are used to generate pseudorandom keystream material.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a nonce is usually correct?
options: It may be public but often must not repeat under the same key
It must always equal the key
It must be kept secret forever
It is another name for plaintext
questions.explanation: Nonce secrecy is usually unnecessary; uniqueness or construction-specific rules matter.
questions.hint: Nonce means number used once.
questions.newbie: Nonce secrecy is usually unnecessary; uniqueness or construction-specific rules matter.
questions.deep: Nonce secrecy is usually unnecessary; uniqueness or construction-specific rules matter.

questions.prompt: What operation commonly combines a stream-cipher keystream with plaintext?
questions.explanation: XOR is efficient and self-inverting: P⊕K⊕K=P.
questions.hint: Think bit-by-bit combination.
questions.newbie: XOR is efficient and self-inverting: P⊕K⊕K=P.
questions.deep: XOR is efficient and self-inverting: P⊕K⊕K=P.

questions.prompt: What should happen if a secure stream cipher uses the same key but a fresh valid nonce for a second message?
options: It should produce a different keystream
It must produce the identical keystream
questions.explanation: A fresh nonce should cause a different keystream under nonce-based stream encryption, preventing keystream reuse.
questions.hint: The nonce exists to vary the encryption instance.

questions.prompt: If the same one-time-pad key encrypts two messages, which secret disappears when the ciphertexts are XORed?
questions.explanation: The pad appears twice and cancels because K⊕K=0.
questions.hint: Write both ciphertext equations and XOR them.
questions.newbie: The pad appears twice and cancels because K⊕K=0.
questions.deep: The pad appears twice and cancels because K⊕K=0.

questions.prompt: Which property must a true one-time-pad key have besides never being reused?
options: It must be truly random and as long as the message
It must be a short memorable password
It must be generated from the plaintext
questions.explanation: Perfect secrecy requires a uniformly random secret pad at least as long as the plaintext and used once.
questions.hint: OTP requirements are stricter than ordinary stream ciphers.
questions.newbie: Perfect secrecy requires a uniformly random secret pad at least as long as the plaintext and used once.
questions.deep: Perfect secrecy requires a uniformly random secret pad at least as long as the plaintext and used once.

questions.prompt: An attacker knows P₁ and sees two ciphertexts encrypted with the same pad. What can the attacker derive?
options: The reused pad segment and corresponding P₂ segment
questions.explanation: From C₁=P₁⊕K, known P₁ reveals K for that segment, which then reveals P₂ from C₂.
questions.hint: XOR a known plaintext with its ciphertext.
questions.newbie: From C₁=P₁⊕K, known P₁ reveals K for that segment, which then reveals P₂ from C₂.
questions.deep: From C₁=P₁⊕K, known P₁ reveals K for that segment, which then reveals P₂ from C₂.

questions.prompt: Which engineering rule prevents the classic two-time-pad failure?
options: Never reuse the pad/keystream for another message
questions.explanation: The central failure is reuse of the same secret keystream material.
questions.hint: The weakness is reuse, not formatting.
questions.newbie: The central failure is reuse of the same secret keystream material.
questions.deep: The central failure is reuse of the same secret keystream material.

questions.prompt: Why can natural-language structure make two-time-pad attacks even worse after C₁⊕C₂ is known?
options: Likely words and character patterns help infer both plaintexts
questions.explanation: Once the pad cancels, language redundancy and guessed words can be used to recover portions of both plaintexts.
questions.hint: Human language contains predictable patterns.

questions.prompt: What is the AES state for a 128-bit data block commonly visualized as?
questions.explanation: AES represents a 16-byte block as a 4×4 state matrix during round transformations.
questions.hint: 128 bits equals 16 bytes.
questions.newbie: AES represents a 16-byte block as a 4×4 state matrix during round transformations.
questions.deep: AES represents a 16-byte block as a 4×4 state matrix during round transformations.

questions.prompt: What does ShiftRows contribute to AES?
options: It moves bytes across columns to help diffusion
It substitutes bytes using the S-box
questions.explanation: ShiftRows rotates rows by different offsets so bytes from one column move into others before MixColumns.
questions.hint: The operation changes byte positions.
questions.newbie: ShiftRows rotates rows by different offsets so bytes from one column move into others before MixColumns.
questions.deep: ShiftRows rotates rows by different offsets so bytes from one column move into others before MixColumns.

questions.prompt: What is the role of AddRoundKey in AES?
options: XOR the state with round-key material
Multiply the key by the plaintext integer
questions.explanation: AddRoundKey combines the state with key-schedule output using XOR.
questions.hint: AES uses XOR to inject key material.
questions.newbie: AddRoundKey combines the state with key-schedule output using XOR.
questions.deep: AddRoundKey combines the state with key-schedule output using XOR.

questions.prompt: AES-256 uses how many encryption rounds?
questions.explanation: AES-256 uses 14 rounds; AES-192 uses 12 and AES-128 uses 10.
questions.hint: Round count increases with key size.
questions.newbie: AES-256 uses 14 rounds; AES-192 uses 12 and AES-128 uses 10.
questions.deep: AES-256 uses 14 rounds; AES-192 uses 12 and AES-128 uses 10.

questions.prompt: Which AES component is primarily responsible for nonlinearity?
questions.explanation: SubBytes applies a nonlinear S-box, preventing AES from being merely a system of linear transformations.
questions.hint: Look for the substitution step.

questions.prompt: CBC encryption needs what extra value for the first block?
questions.explanation: CBC combines the first plaintext block with an initialization vector before encryption.
questions.hint: Chaining needs an initial predecessor.
questions.newbie: CBC combines the first plaintext block with an initialization vector before encryption.
questions.deep: CBC combines the first plaintext block with an initialization vector before encryption.

questions.prompt: What is especially dangerous about reusing a nonce/counter with the same key in CTR mode?
questions.explanation: CTR generates keystream from nonce/counter values, so reuse can repeat keystream material.
questions.hint: CTR behaves like a stream cipher.
questions.newbie: CTR generates keystream from nonce/counter values, so reuse can repeat keystream material.
questions.deep: CTR generates keystream from nonce/counter values, so reuse can repeat keystream material.

questions.prompt: Which modern property does GCM provide when used correctly?
questions.explanation: GCM provides confidentiality plus an authentication tag for integrity/authenticity.
questions.hint: Look for AEAD behavior.
questions.newbie: GCM provides confidentiality plus an authentication tag for integrity/authenticity.
questions.deep: GCM provides confidentiality plus an authentication tag for integrity/authenticity.

questions.prompt: Why is encryption without integrity risky in an active network?
options: An attacker may modify ciphertext without reliable detection
questions.explanation: Confidentiality alone does not necessarily prevent malicious tampering.
questions.hint: Think about active modification rather than eavesdropping.
questions.newbie: Confidentiality alone does not necessarily prevent malicious tampering.
questions.deep: Confidentiality alone does not necessarily prevent malicious tampering.

questions.prompt: What is associated data in an AEAD scheme?
options: A second secret key that must be hidden
questions.explanation: AEAD can authenticate metadata such as headers without encrypting it, binding that data to the ciphertext tag.
questions.hint: It is protected for integrity even though it may remain visible.

questions.prompt: Why do two equal plaintext blocks become equal ciphertext blocks in ECB under one key?
options: Each block is encrypted independently and deterministically
ECB generates a new random key per block
ECB hashes the entire message first
questions.explanation: ECB applies the block cipher independently to each block under the same key.
questions.hint: No chaining value changes the input context.
questions.newbie: ECB applies the block cipher independently to each block under the same key.
questions.deep: ECB applies the block cipher independently to each block under the same key.

questions.prompt: Which kind of data makes ECB pattern leakage especially easy to notice?
options: Structured images or records with repeated blocks
questions.explanation: Repeated structured regions make equality patterns visually or statistically obvious.
questions.hint: Think repeated blocks.
questions.newbie: Repeated structured regions make equality patterns visually or statistically obvious.
questions.deep: Repeated structured regions make equality patterns visually or statistically obvious.

questions.prompt: Does padding ECB with a standard padding scheme solve its repeated-block leakage?
options: Only if the key is public
questions.explanation: Padding handles final block length; it does not add chaining or randomness to equal interior blocks.
questions.hint: Padding and mode security solve different problems.
questions.newbie: Padding handles final block length; it does not add chaining or randomness to equal interior blocks.
questions.deep: Padding handles final block length; it does not add chaining or randomness to equal interior blocks.

questions.prompt: For a new application needing confidentiality and tamper detection, which direction is preferable to ECB?
options: ECB with a shorter block size
questions.explanation: A standardized AEAD scheme protects both confidentiality and integrity when used according to its nonce/key rules.
questions.hint: Prefer authenticated encryption.
questions.newbie: A standardized AEAD scheme protects both confidentiality and integrity when used according to its nonce/key rules.
questions.deep: A standardized AEAD scheme protects both confidentiality and integrity when used according to its nonce/key rules.

questions.prompt: If two database records have an identical 16-byte field and are encrypted with AES-ECB under one key, what can an observer learn?
options: The ciphertext blocks for those equal fields are equal
questions.explanation: ECB reveals equality of repeated plaintext blocks because identical block inputs map to identical ciphertext blocks under the same key.
questions.hint: ECB leaks equality patterns.

questions.prompt: What must remain secret in an ordinary public/private keypair?
questions.explanation: Public-key security assumes the private key is controlled by its owner while the public key may be distributed.
questions.hint: The names are literal.
questions.newbie: Public-key security assumes the private key is controlled by its owner while the public key may be distributed.
questions.deep: Public-key security assumes the private key is controlled by its owner while the public key may be distributed.

questions.prompt: Which task is public-key cryptography particularly useful for compared with purely symmetric systems?
options: Establishing trust or secrets without a pre-shared symmetric key
questions.explanation: Public-key mechanisms help with key establishment, encryption to recipients, and digital signatures.
questions.hint: Think about the initial secret-sharing problem.
questions.newbie: Public-key mechanisms help with key establishment, encryption to recipients, and digital signatures.
questions.deep: Public-key mechanisms help with key establishment, encryption to recipients, and digital signatures.

questions.prompt: Why are public and private keys mathematically related but not interchangeable in practice?
options: They have distinct algorithmic roles and the private value must stay secret
questions.explanation: Keypairs are related by the cryptosystem, but operations and security assumptions assign different roles.
questions.hint: One is distributed; one is protected.
questions.newbie: Keypairs are related by the cryptosystem, but operations and security assumptions assign different roles.
questions.deep: Keypairs are related by the cryptosystem, but operations and security assumptions assign different roles.

questions.prompt: If Alice wants to verify a signature made by Bob, she normally needs…
questions.explanation: Signature verification uses the signer’s public key, with confidence that it actually belongs to the signer.
questions.hint: Verification is a public-key operation.
questions.newbie: Signature verification uses the signer’s public key, with confidence that it actually belongs to the signer.
questions.deep: Signature verification uses the signer’s public key, with confidence that it actually belongs to the signer.

questions.prompt: Why is key authenticity important when distributing a public key?
options: An attacker who substitutes their public key can redirect trust or confidentiality
questions.explanation: A public key may be public, but users still need confidence that it belongs to the intended entity.
questions.hint: Public does not mean unauthenticated.

questions.prompt: Preimage resistance means that given a digest h, it should be hard to…
options: find an input x with H(x)=h
questions.explanation: Preimage resistance protects against reversing a chosen hash output to some matching input.
questions.hint: Start from the digest, not from a message.
questions.newbie: Preimage resistance protects against reversing a chosen hash output to some matching input.
questions.deep: Preimage resistance protects against reversing a chosen hash output to some matching input.

questions.prompt: Second-preimage resistance starts with…
options: one specific message and asks for a different message with the same digest
no messages and asks for any collision
questions.explanation: Second-preimage resistance fixes one input and asks for another distinct input with the same hash.
questions.hint: Differentiate it from arbitrary collision search.
questions.newbie: Second-preimage resistance fixes one input and asks for another distinct input with the same hash.
questions.deep: Second-preimage resistance fixes one input and asks for another distinct input with the same hash.

questions.prompt: Why is a cryptographic hash not the same as encryption?
options: It is designed as a one-way fixed-length mapping with no decryption key
questions.explanation: Hashing is not meant to be reversed with a key; encryption is reversible for authorized parties.
questions.hint: Ask whether there is a decryption operation.
questions.newbie: Hashing is not meant to be reversed with a key; encryption is reversible for authorized parties.
questions.deep: Hashing is not meant to be reversed with a key; encryption is reversible for authorized parties.

questions.prompt: What should happen when the exact same message is hashed twice with the same ordinary hash algorithm?
options: A different random digest is required
questions.explanation: Standard cryptographic hash functions are deterministic.
questions.hint: Same input, same algorithm.
questions.newbie: Standard cryptographic hash functions are deterministic.
questions.deep: Standard cryptographic hash functions are deterministic.

questions.prompt: What is second-preimage resistance?
options: Given one message, it should be hard to find a different message with the same hash
It should be hard to compute any hash
Every message must have a unique mathematical hash forever
A hash must hide its input length
questions.explanation: Second-preimage resistance starts from a specific message and asks for another distinct message with the same digest.
questions.hint: One message is fixed before the attack begins.

questions.prompt: Why are fast general-purpose hashes undesirable for password storage?
options: They let attackers test guesses very quickly
questions.explanation: Password hashing should deliberately increase the cost of each offline guess.
questions.hint: Speed is good for file hashing but bad for password guessing resistance.
questions.newbie: Password hashing should deliberately increase the cost of each offline guess.
questions.deep: Password hashing should deliberately increase the cost of each offline guess.

questions.prompt: Should a password salt normally be stored with the password hash?
options: No, it must be memorized by the user
Only if it equals the password
questions.explanation: A salt is normally public metadata stored alongside the derived password value.
questions.hint: A salt does not rely on secrecy.
questions.newbie: A salt is normally public metadata stored alongside the derived password value.
questions.deep: A salt is normally public metadata stored alongside the derived password value.

questions.prompt: What does a unique salt mainly defeat?
options: Precomputed rainbow-table reuse and equality leakage
questions.explanation: Unique salts force attackers to recompute guesses per record and make equal passwords derive differently.
questions.hint: Think precomputation.
questions.newbie: Unique salts force attackers to recompute guesses per record and make equal passwords derive differently.
questions.deep: Unique salts force attackers to recompute guesses per record and make equal passwords derive differently.

questions.prompt: Which additional defense helps against online password guessing but is separate from password hashing?
questions.explanation: Online controls limit request attempts, while password KDFs mainly raise offline cracking cost.
questions.hint: Distinguish online and offline attackers.
questions.newbie: Online controls limit request attempts, while password KDFs mainly raise offline cracking cost.
questions.deep: Online controls limit request attempts, while password KDFs mainly raise offline cracking cost.

questions.prompt: Why is a memory-hard password hashing function useful?
options: It raises the hardware cost of large-scale offline guessing
It removes the need for salts
It encrypts the entire database automatically
questions.explanation: Memory-hard password hashing increases the resource cost of parallel cracking on GPUs and specialized hardware.
questions.hint: The goal is to make each guess expensive.

questions.prompt: Who commonly issues or derives user private keys in an IBE system?
options: A trusted Private Key Generator / authority
The ciphertext recipient without any secret authority
questions.explanation: IBE relies on a trusted authority with master secret material to derive private keys for identities.
questions.hint: There is a central trust role.
questions.newbie: IBE relies on a trusted authority with master secret material to derive private keys for identities.
questions.deep: IBE relies on a trusted authority with master secret material to derive private keys for identities.

questions.prompt: What convenience can IBE provide compared with conventional certificate lookup?
options: A known identity string can serve as the public identifier
questions.explanation: A sender can use an identity-like string without first retrieving a conventional public-key certificate.
questions.hint: Think email address as public identifier.
questions.newbie: A sender can use an identity-like string without first retrieving a conventional public-key certificate.
questions.deep: A sender can use an identity-like string without first retrieving a conventional public-key certificate.

questions.prompt: Why is compromise of the IBE master secret especially serious?
options: It may enable derivation of many users’ private keys
questions.explanation: The authority’s master secret is a high-value root of trust.
questions.hint: Centralized derivation creates centralized risk.
questions.newbie: The authority’s master secret is a high-value root of trust.
questions.deep: The authority’s master secret is a high-value root of trust.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes IBE from ordinary PKI?
options: IBE can derive public identifiers from identity strings rather than relying on individually certified public keys
questions.explanation: The public-key discovery model differs, while both still require trust and private-key protection.
questions.hint: Focus on how the public key/identifier is obtained.
questions.newbie: The public-key discovery model differs, while both still require trust and private-key protection.
questions.deep: The public-key discovery model differs, while both still require trust and private-key protection.

questions.prompt: What is a central trust concern in many identity-based encryption systems?
options: The private-key generator can derive user private keys
questions.explanation: Because a trusted authority derives user private keys from master secret material, key escrow and authority compromise are important concerns.
questions.hint: Who creates the user private key?

questions.prompt: Ciphertext-policy ABE is useful when access should depend on…
options: a logical policy over user attributes
questions.explanation: CP-ABE lets ciphertext carry a policy that eligible attribute sets can satisfy.
questions.hint: Think role AND department OR clearance.
questions.newbie: CP-ABE lets ciphertext carry a policy that eligible attribute sets can satisfy.
questions.deep: CP-ABE lets ciphertext carry a policy that eligible attribute sets can satisfy.

questions.prompt: An example ABE attribute is…
questions.explanation: Attributes describe users, roles, organizations, clearances, projects, or similar policy facts.
questions.hint: Choose something meaningful for authorization.
questions.newbie: Attributes describe users, roles, organizations, clearances, projects, or similar policy facts.
questions.deep: Attributes describe users, roles, organizations, clearances, projects, or similar policy facts.

questions.prompt: Why can attribute revocation be difficult in ABE?
options: Previously issued key material may reflect attributes that later change
questions.explanation: Attribute/key lifecycle must handle role changes, expiry, and revocation without leaving stale authorization.
questions.hint: What happens after someone leaves a department?
questions.newbie: Attribute/key lifecycle must handle role changes, expiry, and revocation without leaving stale authorization.
questions.deep: Attribute/key lifecycle must handle role changes, expiry, and revocation without leaving stale authorization.

questions.prompt: ABE is best viewed as primarily supporting…
questions.explanation: ABE binds decryption capability to attributes and policies.
questions.hint: Think authorization expressed cryptographically.
questions.newbie: ABE binds decryption capability to attributes and policies.
questions.deep: ABE binds decryption capability to attributes and policies.

questions.prompt: Which example best fits ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption?
options: Encrypt so users with Department=Finance AND Role=Manager can decrypt
Encrypt only to one fixed email address
Hash a password with a salt
Use one AES key for everyone
questions.explanation: Ciphertext-policy ABE embeds an access policy in the ciphertext and users possess attribute-bearing keys.
questions.hint: Look for a policy made from attributes.

questions.prompt: A user proves identity successfully but still cannot open a classified file. Which control is denying access?
questions.explanation: Authentication succeeded; authorization determines whether the authenticated identity has permission.
questions.hint: Identity proof and permission are separate stages.
questions.newbie: Authentication succeeded; authorization determines whether the authenticated identity has permission.
questions.deep: Authentication succeeded; authorization determines whether the authenticated identity has permission.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: Authentication and authorization solve different questions
Authorization proves a password is correct
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions/resources.
questions.hint: Who are you versus what may you do?
questions.newbie: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions/resources.
questions.deep: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions/resources.

questions.prompt: A policy “Finance AND Manager” is an example of…
questions.explanation: The policy determines which attributes/roles are permitted.
questions.hint: It describes permissions, not identity proof.
questions.newbie: The policy determines which attributes/roles are permitted.
questions.deep: The policy determines which attributes/roles are permitted.

questions.prompt: Why does encryption alone not provide complete access management?
options: Systems also need identity, policy, lifecycle, revocation, and enforcement decisions
questions.explanation: Cryptography can enforce parts of access control, but operational identity and policy management remain necessary.
questions.hint: Think beyond the cipher itself.
questions.newbie: Cryptography can enforce parts of access control, but operational identity and policy management remain necessary.
questions.deep: Cryptography can enforce parts of access control, but operational identity and policy management remain necessary.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication checks identity; authorization checks permitted actions
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes who or what the entity is; authorization decides what that authenticated entity may do.
questions.hint: Identity first, permissions second.

questions.prompt: Brute-force key search relies mainly on…
options: trying candidate keys until one works
questions.explanation: Brute force exploits a keyspace small enough, weak enough, or cheap enough to search.
questions.hint: Think exhaustive search.
questions.newbie: Brute force exploits a keyspace small enough, weak enough, or cheap enough to search.
questions.deep: Brute force exploits a keyspace small enough, weak enough, or cheap enough to search.

questions.prompt: A chosen-plaintext attack assumes the attacker can…
options: obtain ciphertexts for plaintexts they choose
questions.explanation: Chosen-input models give the attacker an oracle-like ability to request encryption of selected messages.
questions.hint: The attack name describes what the attacker chooses.
questions.newbie: Chosen-input models give the attacker an oracle-like ability to request encryption of selected messages.
questions.deep: Chosen-input models give the attacker an oracle-like ability to request encryption of selected messages.

questions.prompt: Why are timing differences dangerous in cryptographic code?
options: They can leak information correlated with secret-dependent operations
questions.explanation: Observed execution time can become a side channel if it depends on secrets.
questions.hint: Information can leak outside normal outputs.
questions.newbie: Observed execution time can become a side channel if it depends on secrets.
questions.deep: Observed execution time can become a side channel if it depends on secrets.

questions.prompt: What is a common goal of a replay defense?
questions.explanation: Freshness mechanisms reject old valid messages resent outside their intended context.
questions.hint: Use nonces, counters, or protocol state.
questions.newbie: Freshness mechanisms reject old valid messages resent outside their intended context.
questions.deep: Freshness mechanisms reject old valid messages resent outside their intended context.

questions.prompt: A brute-force attack against a cipher primarily depends on what?
options: The effective keyspace and cost of testing candidates
questions.explanation: Exhaustive search becomes practical when the effective keyspace is too small or candidate testing is cheap.
questions.hint: Think number of possible keys.

questions.prompt: Why must cryptographic protocols define message ordering and context, not only algorithms?
options: Correct primitives can still be misused or replayed in an unsafe protocol flow
questions.explanation: Security depends on how primitives are composed, authenticated, and bound to protocol state.
questions.hint: Strong parts can form a weak whole.
questions.newbie: Security depends on how primitives are composed, authenticated, and bound to protocol state.
questions.deep: Security depends on how primitives are composed, authenticated, and bound to protocol state.

questions.prompt: What does domain separation help prevent?
options: Reusing the same cryptographic value/function context ambiguously across different purposes
questions.explanation: Distinct labels/contexts reduce cross-protocol or cross-purpose confusion.
questions.hint: Bind cryptographic computations to their purpose.
questions.newbie: Distinct labels/contexts reduce cross-protocol or cross-purpose confusion.
questions.deep: Distinct labels/contexts reduce cross-protocol or cross-purpose confusion.

questions.prompt: A protocol accepts a valid MAC from an earlier session as valid now. What property is missing?
questions.explanation: Authentication without freshness can still permit replay across sessions.
questions.hint: A valid old message should not necessarily be valid now.
questions.newbie: Authentication without freshness can still permit replay across sessions.
questions.deep: Authentication without freshness can still permit replay across sessions.

questions.prompt: Why is version negotiation security-sensitive?
options: Attackers may try to force obsolete weaker options
Newer versions always use shorter keys
Negotiation reveals private keys by definition
questions.explanation: Unauthenticated or permissive negotiation can enable downgrade attacks.
questions.hint: Think downgrade.
questions.newbie: Unauthenticated or permissive negotiation can enable downgrade attacks.
questions.deep: Unauthenticated or permissive negotiation can enable downgrade attacks.

questions.prompt: Why can a secure cryptographic primitive still be unsafe inside a protocol?
options: The protocol may misuse nonces, authentication, ordering, or error handling
Secure primitives never work on networks
Only hashes can be used in protocols
questions.explanation: Security depends on composition and state-management rules, not only on the mathematical primitive.
questions.hint: Correct parts can be combined incorrectly.

questions.prompt: What happens if a signed message is modified after signing?
questions.explanation: A valid signature is bound to the signed message data, typically via a cryptographic hash.
questions.hint: Integrity is part of signature verification.
questions.newbie: A valid signature is bound to the signed message data, typically via a cryptographic hash.
questions.deep: A valid signature is bound to the signed message data, typically via a cryptographic hash.

questions.prompt: Which key should a signer protect most carefully?
questions.explanation: Anyone obtaining the signing private key may be able to forge signatures as that key holder.
questions.hint: Signing is the private operation.
questions.newbie: Anyone obtaining the signing private key may be able to forge signatures as that key holder.
questions.deep: Anyone obtaining the signing private key may be able to forge signatures as that key holder.

questions.prompt: Does a digital signature normally hide the message contents?
options: Only if the signature is Base64
questions.explanation: Signatures provide authenticity/integrity evidence, not confidentiality by themselves.
questions.hint: Signing and encryption are distinct.
questions.newbie: Signatures provide authenticity/integrity evidence, not confidentiality by themselves.
questions.deep: Signatures provide authenticity/integrity evidence, not confidentiality by themselves.

questions.prompt: Why is signer public-key authenticity important?
options: Otherwise an attacker could substitute a different verification key
questions.explanation: Verification only proves possession of the private key corresponding to the public key used; identity binding must also be trusted.
questions.hint: Ask how you know whose public key it is.
questions.newbie: Verification only proves possession of the private key corresponding to the public key used; identity binding must also be trusted.
questions.deep: Verification only proves possession of the private key corresponding to the public key used; identity binding must also be trusted.

questions.prompt: When verifying a digital signature, which key is normally used?

Quantum computers reveal passwords by reading RAM remotely
